chapters.n: The story of Esther takes place in Persia, among Jews who stayed in exile rather than returning to Judah. Ahasuerus is usually identified as Xerxes I, who ruled a vast empire from India to Ethiopia.

f.g: The Hebrew form of the Persian name Xšayaršā, known in Greek as Xerxes (reigned 486–465 BC), father of Artaxerxes I.
The Indus River region, in what is now Pakistan.
Hebrew Cush — the region south of Egypt (modern Sudan).

chapters.n: The king rules from Susa, one of Persia’s royal capitals, where Nehemiah later served as cupbearer.

f.g: The citadel of Susa, in what is now southwestern Iran.

chapters.n: In his third year (about 483 BC), the king throws a huge banquet for his officials and military leaders. Many think this gathering may have been connected to planning his war against Greece.

f.g: The two peoples that formed the core of the empire.

f.g: Their customs differ — they worship one God and keep the Sabbath and dietary laws.

f.w: on the prey they laid not their hand

chapters.n: Across the empire, Jews defend themselves and gain rest from their enemies, killing 75,000 attackers. Once more, the text stresses that they took no plunder.

f.g: Defended themselves.

chapters.n: In the provinces the fighting is on the thirteenth, and they rest and celebrate on the fourteenth.

f.w: made it a day of feasting and gladness
f.g: The origin of the feast of Purim.

chapters.n: In Susa the fighting lasted two days, so the Jews there celebrated on the fifteenth. This explains why Purim falls on two different dates.

f.w: on the fifteenth day of the same they rested
f.g: Still today, walled cities like Jerusalem celebrate “Shushan Purim” on the 15th of Adar.

chapters.n: So village Jews celebrated on the fourteenth with feasting and sending gifts of food to one another — a custom still practiced at Purim.

f.g: Gifts of food, still exchanged at Purim today.
Open villages without walls.

chapters.n: Mordecai writes to Jews near and far to record what happened.

f.g: Near and far.

chapters.n: He establishes an annual two-day celebration on the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar.

f.g: Establish.

chapters.n: These days remember when sorrow turned to joy and mourning to celebration. They are to include feasting, gifts to friends, and gifts to the poor — joy that reaches out to others.
The Jews accept Mordecai’s instructions and continue the celebration they had begun.
A summary of the story: Haman, enemy of all the Jews, plotted to destroy them and cast Pur (the lot) to choose the day.
But when the matter came before the king, Haman’s evil plan turned back on his own head.

f.w: should return upon his own head

chapters.n: The feast is named Purim, from “Pur,” the lot Haman cast. The name itself is a reminder that what seemed like chance was overruled by God.

f.g: Plural of “pur” — “lots.”

chapters.n: The Jews commit themselves, their children, and any who join them to keep these two days every year without fail.

f.w: took upon them, and upon their seed
f.g: Bound themselves and their descendants.

f.w: all such as joined themselves unto them

chapters.n: Purim is to be remembered in every generation, family, province, and city. Remembering God’s deliverances helps faith endure.

f.w: remembered and kept throughout every generation

chapters.n: Queen Esther, with Mordecai, writes with full authority to confirm the festival. Esther, once hidden, now speaks with royal authority for her people.

f.g: With full official power.

chapters.n: The letters go to all 127 provinces with “words of peace and truth” — a greeting of well-being and faithfulness.
The letters confirm the dates of Purim, along with remembrance of the fasting and lamenting that preceded the deliverance. Today a fast, the “Fast of Esther,” comes the day before Purim.

f.w: the matters of the fastings and their cry

f.g: Commanded.

chapters.n: Esther’s decree makes these rules official, and they are written down in the records. Her leadership closes the story of Purim.

f.w: it was written in the book
f.g: Recorded in an official book, perhaps the royal or community records.

chapters.n: The book closes by noting the king’s power: he imposed taxes across his empire, even on distant coastlands. Life in the empire went on — but now with a faithful Jew at the king’s side.

f.g: Taxes or forced labor.
Coastlands and islands, such as those in the Mediterranean.

chapters.n: The king’s deeds and Mordecai’s greatness were recorded in the official chronicles of Persia — a formula like those used for Israel’s kings, inviting readers to see this as real history.

f.w: are they not written in the book of the chronicles

chapters.n: Mordecai becomes second only to the king and is loved by his people. He used his power to seek their good and speak peace for their future — a model of righteous leadership.

f.w: seeking the wealth of his people
f.g: Working for the welfare and good of his people.

f.w: speaking peace to all his seed
f.g: Speaking up for the peace and well-being of all his descendants.
